_doc: Completed T-0485 ledger. Every frozen-manifest member received a dated repository/source-register review and targeted exact/variant-name web sweep. Unlisted overrides use the documented no-corroboration default; pending is empty.
default_summary: No reliable record in the reviewed repository corpus and targeted exact/variant-name web sweep could be tied to this postal person with sufficient date/place discriminators. This is a documented no-corroboration result, not evidence that the person did not exist.

ll_parsons_edward.summary: An Edward Parsons appears in the 1839 Chicago voter material embedded with Fergus-era directory material. Exact-name later Chicago evidence is useful but too late to prove the 1834 postal identity.

candidates.basis: Exact Edward Parsons appears among 1839 Chicago voters.
conflicts: Five-year gap and common surname; no 1834-35 identity bridge.

ll_paul_kingston.summary: Independent early-Chicago sources identify Paul Kingston as a Chicago landholder; a Racine old-settlers record says he came from Chicago on January 2, 1835. This strongly corroborates the rare named Chicago person, while indicating movement to Racine before the July scene date.

ll_phineas_how.summary: A Phineas Howe is recorded as coming from New York to Illinois in 1835 and settling near Marengo. The spelling is close, but the geography is outside Chicago and the exact arrival timing is not enough for a merge.

candidates.basis: Rare given name and near-exact surname variant in northern Illinois in 1835.
conflicts: Marengo geography; source spells Howe; no direct postal bridge.

ll_pierce_downer.summary: Pierce Downer is independently documented visiting Fort Dearborn/Chicago in 1832 and then founding Downers Grove. The exact rare name and regional chronology make this a strong identity candidate, but his established Downers Grove residence prevents treating the postal seed as a Chicago household.

candidates.basis: Downers Grove Historical Society documents 1832 Chicago visit and Downers Grove settlement.
conflicts: Established residence west of Chicago from 1832 onward.

ll_r_c_bristol.summary: The 1839 Chicago directory lists Robert C. Bristol as a forwarding/commission merchant at State and South Water. Initials align with the 1834 R. C. Bristol seed, but the later date leaves identity unresolved.

candidates.basis: Exact initials expand naturally to Robert C.; Chicago merchant in 1839.
conflicts: Five-year gap; no direct 1834 record found.

ll_ruel_starr.summary: Porter County histories place Ruel Starr in Indiana by 1833/1834, where he remained and became a county official. This is a strong same-name competing identity and argues against silently treating the 1834 Chicago letter as Chicago residence.

candidates.basis: Rare exact name, correct frontier timeframe.
conflicts: Documented Porter County, Indiana settlement and continued residence.

ll_salmon_rutherford.summary: Grundy County history identifies Salmon Rutherford as the first permanent Aux Sable settler in May 1833, later operating a tavern/stage stop. The rare exact name strongly matches a regional person but establishes non-Chicago residence.

candidates.basis: Rare exact name in northeastern Illinois by 1833.
conflicts: Aux Sable/Grundy County residence is explicitly documented.

ll_samuel_brookes.summary: Fergus' 1839 Chicago directory lists Samuel Brookes, florist, on Adams Street near Dearborn. The exact spelling is useful later evidence but does not resolve the May 1835 postal identity.

ll_samuel_s_lathrop.summary: Andreas' history of Chicago's First Baptist Church names Samuel S. Lathrop as one of the church's early members after its October 1833 organization and records him building the fence around Rev. A. B. Freeman's Chicago grave. This independently corroborates the exact named Chicago resident before the 1835 postal seed.

ll_sciota_evans.summary: A Cook County history quoting the Chicago Democrat's October 15, 1834 political list names Sciota Evans among leading Cook County Democratic-Republicans. Milwaukee records then show Sciota Evans as constable in September 1835, documenting a plausible migration after the Chicago postal seed.

ll_thomas_andrus.summary: DuPage history gives a detailed chronology for Thomas Andrus: arrival in Chicago Dec. 1, 1833, carpenter/pile-driving work in 1834, return east in autumn 1834, and arrival back at Chicago in June 1835 before settling in DuPage in July. This independently identifies the exact person behind the regional postal seed.

ll_thomas_conger.summary: A Thomas Conger served as a Michigan village clerk in 1835 and president in 1836. This is a contemporaneous competing namesake, but there is no evidence connecting him to the Chicago postal entry.

candidates.basis: Exact contemporaneous name in Great Lakes region.
conflicts: Michigan office and no Chicago bridge; name not rare enough for merge.

ll_thos_fitzgerald.summary: A Thomas Fitzgerald served as president of a Berrien County, Michigan village in 1834. This contemporaneous namesake is retained only as a competing candidate; no link to the Chicago postal person is established.

candidates.basis: Exact contemporaneous name in Great Lakes region.
conflicts: Michigan geography and common name; no Chicago bridge.

ll_william_luce.summary: Racine County old-settlers history says William Luce was already in Captain Knapp's cabin at Racine when a party came from Chicago on January 2, 1835. The rare exact name and regional chronology are strong, but this evidence points away from Chicago residence at the May 1835 postal date.

candidates.basis: Exact name in January 1835 southeastern Wisconsin pioneer account.
conflicts: Documented at Racine before the May 1835 Chicago letter list.

ll_winthrop_merrill.summary: The repository already contains a separate ll_merrill_winthrop postal person, making this likely a transposed-name duplicate requiring adjudication. Local history also places Winthrop Merrill with his family in the Chicago/Jefferson Township migration context by the mid-1830s.

candidates.basis: Exact name components reversed in another repository resident; local history places Winthrop Merrill in early Chicago-area migration.
conflicts: Two stable IDs exist and should not be merged silently; some histories date township settlement to 1836.

ll_wm_h_fraser.summary: Wm. H. Fraser and Wm. H. Frazer are separate stable postal IDs in the same cohort only weeks apart in early 1834. The one-letter surname variation is a strong duplicate/transcription lead, but no external identity discriminator was found.

candidates.basis: Near-identical full initials/name and closely spaced 1834 postal dates.
conflicts: No independent source yet resolves whether one or two people.

ll_wm_h_frazer.summary: Wm. H. Frazer and Wm. H. Fraser are separate stable postal IDs in the same cohort only weeks apart in early 1834. The one-letter surname variation is a strong duplicate/transcription lead, but no external identity discriminator was found.

candidates.basis: Near-identical full initials/name and closely spaced 1834 postal dates.
conflicts: No independent source yet resolves whether one or two people.

ll_wm_osborn.summary: Will County history places a William Osborn among Thorn Creek settlers in 1833-34. This is geographically plausible for a Chicago post-office contact, but the common name and Will County residence are insufficient for a merge.

conflicts: Will County geography and common name; no direct Chicago bridge.
